analysis.one_liner: Replaces federal income taxes with a flat 17% tax on wages while leaving investment income untaxed and repealing the estate tax.
analysis.headline: The flat tax bill had no cosponsors and died in the Senate Finance Committee without ever getting a markup or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would throw out the current income tax and replace it with one flat 17% rate. Only wages, retirement payouts, and unemployment checks would count as taxable income, after a fairly large standard deduction. Money from investments — interest, dividends, capital gains, rents — would not be taxed at the individual level at all. It would also repeal the estate tax, the alternative minimum tax, every federal income tax credit (including the earned income tax credit), and the rules that stop company retirement plans from favoring executives, and it would lock the 17% rate in with a three-fifths supermajority requirement for any future tax increase.
analysis.who_benefits: Households whose wealth comes from investments rather than paychecks would see that income go untaxed. The owners of the largest estates would no longer pay estate or gift tax. Employers with overfunded pension plans could pull excess assets back to the company with the old penalty tax repealed. High-income employees would also benefit from repeal of the alternative minimum tax and of limits on retirement plans.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Wealthy investors and the largest estates

how_it_helps.text: Sets a single 17% rate on individual taxable income, defined only as wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment compensation above a standard deduction ($14,480 single, $28,960 joint), and repeals all other income tax rates and most income tax provisions.
Taxes business activity at 17% and imposes the tax on the person engaged in the business whether an individual, partnership, or corporation, ending the separate corporate tax.
Repeals the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes for deaths and gifts after December 31, 2015, and repeals the alternative minimum tax.

Repeals pension plan rules on nondiscrimination, contribution limits, and restrictions on distributions, and repeals the tax on employers reclaiming excess pension assets, allowing such transfers with only ordinary income inclusion.

Declares it out of order in either chamber to consider any bill raising an income tax rate, cutting the standard deduction, or adding any tax benefit, waivable only by a three-fifths vote — locking the flat tax in against future change.

analysis.who_pays: Wage earners, who would pay 17% on everything they earn above the standard deduction. Low- and moderate-income working families would lose the earned income tax credit, child tax credit, and every other income tax credit. The Treasury would lose the revenue from the estate tax and from taxes on investment income, which someone would eventually have to make up. Hospitals, universities, and federal, state, and local governments would owe a new 17% tax on the value of benefits like health insurance they provide employees.
analysis.who_pays_short: Wage earners, working families, and government budgets

drawbacks.text: Taxable income counts only wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment compensation — interest, dividends, capital gains, and rental income are left out entirely, so income from wealth would go untaxed while income from work is taxed at 17%.

The bill repeals all income tax credits, including the earned income tax credit and child tax credit, which would raise taxes on low- and moderate-income working families even as the flat rate lowers bills for high earners.

Repealing the nondiscrimination, minimum participation, and contribution limit rules for retirement plans removes the safeguards that keep company pension and 401(k) plans from being designed mostly for highly paid executives.

The supermajority lock makes it nearly impossible for a future Congress to raise the tax rate or restore repealed benefits, entrenching this distribution of the tax burden beyond a normal majority vote.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Simplification is real: one rate, one deduction, and no alternative minimum tax would make filing dramatically easier, and the standard deduction would shield lower earners from the rate itself. But the design decides who wins: it taxes only income from work and leaves income from investments untaxed, repeals the estate tax, and strips out the credits that working families rely on. The net effect is a large shift of the tax burden from concentrated wealth onto wages, and the supermajority provision would make that shift very hard to reverse.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Shelby introduced it in April 2015 and it went straight to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up; with no cosponsors and no further action, it expired when the Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 14, 2015 and read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day.
It never received a markup, a committee vote, or floor action, and no legislator cosponsored it.
No further action was taken before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained anything, because the bill never advanced. Working families and taxpayers generally are better off that it died, since it would have untaxed investment income and repealed credits they rely on; the existing graduated tax and the estate tax remained in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Working families — the bill never advanced

for.name: Sen. Richard Shelby
for.role: U.S. Senator from Alabama and sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the flat tax bill and offered no cosponsors; the bill went to the Finance Committee and received no further action.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee (Chair Orrin Hatch)
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no markup, no committee vote, no report — leaving it to expire at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes or cosponsors to measure support: a single Republican senator sponsored the bill and no member of either party signed on.

industries.industry: High-income households and the largest estates
industries.note: The bill would leave interest, dividends, capital gains, and rents untaxed at the individual level and repeal the estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes entirely. The benefit flows to people whose income comes from wealth; the revenue those taxes raise would have to come from someone else.

With capital income untaxed for individuals, the tax code would stop reaching the returns on investment portfolios and financial assets. Funds and brokers would operate in a largely tax-free zone for their clients' gains.

The bill repeals the penalty tax on employers taking back 'excess' pension assets and allows such transfers with only ordinary income inclusion. Company treasuries could reclaim pension plan money, with plan participants protected mainly by the vesting rules.

industries.industry: Nonprofits, hospitals, universities, and federal, state, and local governments
industries.note: These employers would owe a new 17% tax on the value of noncash compensation — chiefly health insurance and other fringe benefits — they provide their employees, a cost that does not fall on private, for-profit businesses.
